questions.question: An organization is structured so that team members report primarily to functional managers, and the project manager has little authority and must negotiate for resources. Which organizational structure is this?
questions.explanation:
In a Functional structure, staff report to functional managers and the project manager has minimal authority, often acting only as a coordinator who must negotiate for resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
Projectized: in a projectized structure the project manager has high authority and team members report directly to the PM, the opposite of this scenario.
Strong matrix: a strong matrix gives the PM significant authority over resources, which contradicts the limited authority described.
Balanced matrix: a balanced matrix shares authority roughly equally between functional and project managers, more than the PM has here.

questions.question: A project manager in a projectized organization is wondering what authority level they have over the budget and team. What is TRUE of the project manager's authority in a projectized structure?
options: The PM has little to no authority
The PM has high to total authority over resources and budget
The PM only coordinates and cannot direct staff
The PM shares authority equally with functional managers
questions.explanation:
The PM has high to total authority over resources and budget in a projectized organization, where teams are organized around projects and report directly to the project manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
The PM has little to no authority: that describes a functional structure, not a projectized one.
The PM shares authority equally with functional managers: equal sharing describes a balanced matrix, not a projectized structure.
The PM only coordinates and cannot direct staff: a coordinator role with no direction power is characteristic of a weak/functional structure.

questions.question: Which framework is a process-improvement approach that uses DMAIC to reduce defects and process variation?
questions.explanation:
Six Sigma is a data-driven quality methodology that uses the DMAIC cycle (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) to reduce defects and variation.

Why the other options are wrong:
PRINCE2: PRINCE2 is a structured project management methodology, not a defect-reduction statistical approach.
SAFe: the Scaled Agile Framework coordinates Agile across large enterprises and does not center on DMAIC defect reduction.
ITIL: ITIL is a set of IT service management best practices, unrelated to the DMAIC process-improvement cycle.

questions.question: A large enterprise needs to coordinate dozens of Agile teams working on one product, aligning their cadences and dependencies. Which framework is designed for this scale?
questions.explanation:
SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) is purpose-built to coordinate many Agile teams across a large enterprise, aligning their cadences, dependencies, and releases.

Why the other options are wrong:
Kanban: Kanban manages flow for a single team or value stream and does not provide enterprise-wide multi-team coordination.
Scrum: standard Scrum governs one team and lacks built-in mechanisms to align dozens of teams.
Lean: Lean is a philosophy for eliminating waste, not a structured framework for scaling many Agile teams.

questions.question: A project uses fixed-length iterations, daily stand-ups, and a backlog reviewed each cycle, but the team also wants to limit work in progress and visualize flow on a board. The PM blends two approaches. This hybrid is BEST described as:
questions.explanation:
Scrumban blends Scrum's iterations, roles, and backlog with Kanban's work-in-progress limits and flow visualization, exactly the hybrid described.

Why the other options are wrong:
PRINCE2: PRINCE2 is a predictive, process-based methodology, not a Scrum-Kanban blend.
Waterfall with gates: gated Waterfall is sequential and does not use backlogs, stand-ups, or WIP limits.
Pure Kanban: pure Kanban has no fixed iterations or sprint backlog, both of which this team retained from Scrum.

questions.question: A PMO is being established that sets standards and provides templates and training but lets individual project managers retain control of their projects. Which PMO type is this?
questions.explanation:
A Supportive PMO provides templates, training, and best practices in a consultative role while project managers keep control of their own projects.

Why the other options are wrong:
Directive PMO: a directive PMO takes direct control of projects by managing them itself, which removes PM autonomy.
Controlling PMO: a controlling PMO mandates compliance with specific frameworks and methods, exerting more authority than a supportive one.
Functional PMO: functional PMO is not a standard PMO classification under this model.

questions.question: In Agile, what is the primary purpose of a sprint review?
options: To plan the work for the upcoming sprint
To remove impediments blocking the team
To reflect on team processes and improve them
To demonstrate the completed increment to stakeholders for feedback
questions.explanation:
The sprint review exists To demonstrate the completed increment to stakeholders for feedback, inspecting the product and adapting the backlog.

Why the other options are wrong:
To plan the work for the upcoming sprint: that is sprint planning, a separate event held before the sprint begins.
To reflect on team processes and improve them: that describes the sprint retrospective, which focuses on the team rather than the product.
To remove impediments blocking the team: removing impediments is the Scrum Master's ongoing duty, not the goal of the review.

questions.question: In Agile, what is a sprint?
options: A document listing all project requirements
The final phase of a Waterfall project
A short, fixed time-boxed iteration in which a usable increment is produced
questions.explanation:
A sprint is A short, fixed time-boxed iteration in which a usable increment is produced, typically one to four weeks long.

Why the other options are wrong:
A document listing all project requirements: that describes a requirements document or backlog, not a time-boxed iteration.
A meeting to resolve impediments: impediment resolution happens during stand-ups and the Scrum Master's work, not as the definition of a sprint.
The final phase of a Waterfall project: sprints are an Agile concept and have no place in Waterfall phases.

questions.question: A project must integrate a fixed-scope hardware component with strict regulatory gates, while the accompanying software UI evolves with user feedback. Which approach BEST handles both parts?
options: A hybrid life cycle combining predictive and adaptive approaches
questions.explanation:
A hybrid life cycle combining predictive and adaptive approaches lets the fixed hardware follow predictive phase gates while the evolving software UI is built iteratively.

Why the other options are wrong:
Pure Waterfall for everything: forcing the evolving UI into rigid Waterfall would prevent the iterative feedback the software needs.
Pure Agile for everything: applying pure Agile to fixed-scope, regulated hardware ignores the required gates and stable scope.
Big bang delivery: delivering everything at once provides no phase control for hardware nor iteration for software.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a daily stand-up (daily scrum) in Agile?
options: For the team to synchronize and surface impediments in a brief meeting
To create the entire project schedule
To demonstrate the product to customers
questions.explanation:
The daily stand-up is held For the team to synchronize and surface impediments in a brief meeting, typically time-boxed to 15 minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
To formally approve change requests: change approval is handled through change control, not the daily scrum.
To demonstrate the product to customers: product demonstrations occur at the sprint review, not the stand-up.
To create the entire project schedule: the schedule is built during planning, not in a brief daily sync.

questions.question: A team estimates backlog items using relative story points rather than hours. Over several sprints they measure the average points completed per sprint. This average is used primarily to:
options: Forecast how much work future sprints can deliver (velocity)
questions.explanation:
The average story points completed per sprint is velocity, used to Forecast how much work future sprints can deliver (velocity) and predict release timing.

Why the other options are wrong:
Calculate earned value: earned value uses cost and schedule baselines in dollars, not relative story points per sprint.
Determine the critical path: the critical path comes from network diagram analysis of dependent activities, not sprint velocity.
Set the procurement budget: velocity measures delivery capacity, not procurement spending.

questions.question: Which Agile artifact is an ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product, maintained by the product owner?
questions.explanation:
The Product backlog is the single, ordered list of all desired features and work for the product, owned and prioritized by the product owner.

Why the other options are wrong:
Sprint backlog: the sprint backlog is the subset of items selected for the current sprint, not the full product list.
Burndown chart: a burndown chart visualizes remaining work over time, not a list of requirements.
Definition of done: the definition of done is the shared quality checklist for completion, not the backlog itself.

questions.question: Which group is typically responsible for reviewing and approving or rejecting formal change requests on a project?
questions.explanation:
The change control board (CCB) reviews submitted change requests and formally approves, defers, or rejects them based on impact analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
The project sponsor alone: while a sponsor may sit on the board, change decisions are made through the CCB process, not by one person in isolation.
The vendor's account manager: a vendor representative does not have authority to approve changes to the customer's project baseline.
The end users: end users may request changes but do not formally approve them.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a change control process on a project?
options: To eliminate the need for a project schedule
To speed up delivery by skipping reviews
To ensure changes are evaluated, approved, and documented before implementation
To prevent any changes from ever occurring
questions.explanation:
Change control exists To ensure changes are evaluated, approved, and documented before implementation, protecting baselines and managing impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
To prevent any changes from ever occurring: change control manages change in an orderly way, it does not forbid all change.
To speed up delivery by skipping reviews: skipping reviews defeats the purpose of controlled, evaluated change.
To eliminate the need for a project schedule: a schedule remains essential and is in fact one of the baselines change control protects.

questions.question: An emergency production outage requires an immediate fix that cannot wait for the next scheduled CCB meeting. What is the BEST course of action under change control?
options: Wait two weeks for the next CCB meeting
Make the fix and never document it
Invoke an expedited or emergency change approval, then document it
questions.explanation:
The PM should Invoke an expedited or emergency change approval, then document it, using the predefined emergency change path and recording it retroactively.

Why the other options are wrong:
Make the fix and never document it: skipping documentation violates governance and leaves baselines and records inaccurate.
Wait two weeks for the next CCB meeting: waiting prolongs a critical outage and is unacceptable for an emergency.
Cancel the project: canceling the project is a drastic, unrelated overreaction to an operational outage.

questions.question: A risk is identified with very low probability and minimal impact, so the team decides to take no proactive action but to deal with it if it occurs. This response is:
questions.explanation:
Taking no proactive action and handling the risk only if it materializes is the Accept strategy, appropriate for low-priority risks.

Why the other options are wrong:
Avoid: avoidance requires changing the plan to remove the risk, which is unnecessary effort for a trivial risk.
Mitigate: mitigation spends resources reducing probability or impact, more than this minor risk warrants.
Exploit: exploit is a response for positive risks (opportunities), not for a negative risk being accepted.

questions.question: A risk has a 20% probability of occurring and would cost $50,000 if it does. What is the expected monetary value (EMV) of this risk?
questions.explanation:
$10,000 is correct because EMV equals probability times impact: 0.20 multiplied by $50,000 equals $10,000.

Why the other options are wrong:
$50,000: $50,000 is the full impact if the risk occurs, but EMV weights that impact by its 20% probability.
$70,000: $70,000 incorrectly adds the probability percentage to the impact instead of multiplying.
$2,500: $2,500 results from a calculation error and does not equal 0.20 times $50,000.

questions.question: A project manager wants to perform a Monte Carlo simulation and assign dollar values to risks to model overall project cost uncertainty. This effort is BEST classified as:
questions.explanation:
Assigning numeric dollar values and running Monte Carlo simulations to model cost uncertainty is Quantitative risk analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
Qualitative risk analysis: qualitative analysis uses subjective ratings like High/Low, not numeric simulations and dollar values.
Risk identification: identification finds and lists risks but does not assign numeric impact or run simulations.
Risk avoidance: avoidance is a response strategy, not an analysis technique.

questions.question: A positive risk (opportunity) could let the project finish early if a vendor delivers ahead of schedule. The team takes action to ensure this opportunity is realized by guaranteeing the early delivery. Which response strategy is this?
questions.explanation:
Exploit is the opportunity response that takes action to ensure the positive risk definitely happens, such as guaranteeing the early vendor delivery.

Why the other options are wrong:
Enhance: enhancing increases the probability or impact of an opportunity but does not guarantee it will occur.
Share: sharing allocates the opportunity to a third party best able to capture it, not directly securing it.
Accept: accepting takes no proactive action to make the opportunity happen.

questions.question: During which stage of risk management does the team brainstorm, review documents, and use techniques like SWOT analysis to discover potential risks?
questions.explanation:
Risk identification is the stage where the team uses brainstorming, document reviews, and SWOT analysis to discover and list potential risks.

Why the other options are wrong:
Risk response planning: response planning develops strategies for already-identified risks, not the discovery of new ones.
Quantitative analysis: quantitative analysis numerically evaluates risks that have already been identified.
Risk monitoring: monitoring tracks known risks and watches for new ones during execution, after identification.

questions.question: A project manager sets aside a budget reserve to handle risks that have been identified and analyzed. This reserve is BEST described as a:
questions.explanation:
A Contingency reserve is funding set aside to address identified, analyzed risks that may occur, and it is controlled by the project manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
Management reserve: management reserve covers unknown-unknown risks and is controlled by management, not for identified risks.
Cost baseline: the cost baseline is the approved spending plan including contingency, not the reserve itself.
Profit margin: profit margin is the financial gain on a contract, unrelated to project risk reserves.

questions.question: Which field is MOST important to include in an issue log to ensure each issue is resolved?
options: The color preference of the stakeholder
The issue owner responsible for resolution
questions.explanation:
The issue owner responsible for resolution is essential so that accountability is clear and each issue is actively driven to closure.

Why the other options are wrong:
The color preference of the stakeholder: cosmetic preferences are irrelevant to resolving an issue.
The vendor's stock price: a vendor's stock price has no bearing on tracking and closing a project issue.
The project's start date: while useful project metadata, the start date does not drive resolution of an individual issue.

questions.question: An issue is too large for the project team to resolve and exceeds the project manager's authority. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Escalate the issue to the sponsor or appropriate authority
Reassign it to a junior team member
Remove it from the issue log
questions.explanation:
When an issue exceeds the PM's authority, the correct action is to Escalate the issue to the sponsor or appropriate authority who can make the necessary decision.

Why the other options are wrong:
Resolve it without authority: acting beyond one's authority risks unauthorized decisions and accountability problems.
Remove it from the issue log: removing the issue hides a real problem rather than resolving it.
Reassign it to a junior team member: a junior member also lacks the authority the issue requires, so this does not help.

questions.question: What is the purpose of assigning a priority level to each item in an issue log?
options: To decide which issues to ignore permanently
To determine the order and urgency in which issues are addressed
questions.explanation:
Assigning priority helps To determine the order and urgency in which issues are addressed, ensuring the most critical problems get attention first.

Why the other options are wrong:
To decide which issues to ignore permanently: prioritization sequences issues, it does not authorize ignoring them.
To set the project budget: the budget is established during cost planning, not by issue priority.
To replace the risk register: the issue log and risk register serve different purposes and do not replace each other.

questions.question: A project manager reviews the issue log in the weekly status meeting and finds several issues marked open for many weeks with no progress. What is the BEST action?
options: Close all old issues to clean up the log
Review each stalled issue, reassign or escalate, and set resolution dates
questions.explanation:
The PM should Review each stalled issue, reassign or escalate, and set resolution dates to drive accountability and unblock progress.

Why the other options are wrong:
Close all old issues to clean up the log: closing unresolved issues hides real problems rather than resolving them.
Delete the issue log: deleting the log eliminates critical tracking and accountability.
Stop holding status meetings: status meetings are how stalled issues surface; stopping them worsens visibility.

questions.question: An issue log entry should include a target resolution date primarily to:
options: Hold the owner accountable and track whether resolution is on time
questions.explanation:
A target resolution date helps Hold the owner accountable and track whether resolution is on time, providing a deadline to measure progress against.

Why the other options are wrong:
Decorate the document: a date serves a functional tracking purpose, not decoration.
Calculate the critical path: the critical path is derived from schedule activities, not issue resolution dates.
Determine vendor payment terms: payment terms come from procurement contracts, not the issue log.

questions.question: In a WBS, the lowest level of decomposition, where cost and duration can be reliably estimated, is called a:
questions.explanation:
The lowest level of the WBS is the Work package, where work can be scheduled, estimated for cost and duration, and assigned.

Why the other options are wrong:
Milestone: a milestone is a significant point in time with zero duration, not a unit of work to estimate.
Phase gate: a phase gate is a decision checkpoint between phases, not a WBS element.
Deliverable summary: a summary level aggregates work packages but is not the lowest estimable level.

questions.question: A milestone in a project schedule is BEST described as:
options: A task with a long duration
A significant point or event in the project with zero duration
questions.explanation:
A milestone is A significant point or event in the project with zero duration, marking key achievements such as a phase completion.

Why the other options are wrong:
A task with a long duration: a milestone has no duration, unlike a work task.
A budget reserve: a budget reserve is funding set aside, not a schedule point.
A risk response: a risk response is an action to address a risk, unrelated to a schedule milestone.

questions.question: A project network has a single path: Activity A (3 days) to B (5 days) to C (2 days) to D (4 days), all in sequence with finish-to-start dependencies. What is the project's total duration along this critical path?
questions.explanation:
14 days is correct because the activities are sequential, so the duration is 3 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 14 days, which is the critical path length.

Why the other options are wrong:
10 days: 10 days omits one or more activities from the sum of 3 + 5 + 2 + 4.
12 days: 12 days is an incorrect partial total and does not include all four sequential durations.
9 days: 9 days drops the longest activity and undercounts the path total.

questions.question: Two paths lead to project completion: Path 1 (A=4, B=6, C=3) totals 13 days, and Path 2 (A=4, D=5, C=3) totals 12 days. Activity D has how many days of total float?
questions.explanation:
1 day is correct because Path 2 (12 days) is one day shorter than the critical Path 1 (13 days), giving its non-shared activity D exactly 1 day of float.

Why the other options are wrong:
0 days: 0 days would mean D is on the critical path, but Path 2 is shorter, so D has slack.
5 days: 5 days is simply D's duration, not its float, which is the difference between path lengths.
13 days: 13 days is the critical path total, not the float of activity D.

questions.question: In the critical path method, the critical path is BEST defined as:
options: The path with the most activities
The longest path through the network, which determines the minimum project duration
The shortest path through the network
The path with the largest total float
questions.explanation:
The longest path through the network, which determines the minimum project duration defines the critical path; any delay on it delays the whole project.

Why the other options are wrong:
The shortest path through the network: the shortest path is not critical because it has slack and does not drive completion.
The path with the most activities: the number of activities is irrelevant; total duration determines criticality.
The path with the largest total float: critical path activities have zero float, not the largest float.

questions.question: A project manager estimates an activity using optimistic (O), most likely (M), and pessimistic (P) values with the formula (O + 4M + P) / 6. This three-point technique is known as:
questions.explanation:
PERT (beta) estimating uses the weighted three-point formula (O + 4M + P) / 6 to produce an expected activity duration.

Why the other options are wrong:
Analogous estimating: analogous estimating uses data from similar past projects, not a three-point formula.
Parametric estimating: parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by quantity, not the weighted O/M/P average.
Bottom-up estimating: bottom-up estimating sums detailed work package estimates rather than applying a three-point formula.

questions.question: For an activity, the optimistic estimate is 4 days, most likely is 10 days, and pessimistic is 22 days. Using the PERT formula (O + 4M + P) / 6, what is the expected duration?
questions.explanation:
11 days is correct because (4 + 4 times 10 + 22) / 6 = (4 + 40 + 22) / 6 = 66 / 6 = 11 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
12 days: 12 days is a simple average of the three values, not the PERT weighted formula.
10 days: 10 days is the most likely value alone, ignoring the optimistic and pessimistic weighting.
13 days: 13 days does not result from the correct (4 + 40 + 22) / 6 calculation.

questions.question: A project manager estimates a new project's cost by referencing the actual cost of a similar completed project. This top-down technique is called:
questions.explanation:
Analogous estimating uses the actual values from a similar past project to estimate the current one, a quick top-down method.

Why the other options are wrong:
Bottom-up estimating: bottom-up sums detailed estimates of each work package, the opposite of a top-down reference.
Three-point estimating: three-point estimating uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values, not a single past project.
Reserve analysis: reserve analysis sets aside contingency funds, not an estimating technique based on past projects.

questions.question: A project is behind schedule. The PM decides to overlap two activities that were originally planned to run sequentially. This schedule compression technique is:
questions.explanation:
Fast tracking compresses the schedule by performing activities in parallel that were planned sequentially, accepting added risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
Crashing: crashing shortens the schedule by adding resources to critical activities, not by overlapping them.
Leveling: resource leveling adjusts the schedule to address resource constraints and may even lengthen it.
Resource smoothing: smoothing adjusts activities within available float and does not compress the overall schedule by overlapping.

questions.question: What does a service level agreement (SLA) define?
options: The order of WBS work packages
The agreed level of service, such as uptime or response time, between a provider and customer
questions.explanation:
An SLA defines The agreed level of service, such as uptime or response time, between a provider and customer, with measurable targets and consequences.

Why the other options are wrong:
The team's daily stand-up schedule: a stand-up schedule is an internal team practice, not a service commitment.
The project's risk responses: risk responses are documented in the risk register, not an SLA.
The order of WBS work packages: work sequencing is a scheduling concern, unrelated to service levels.

questions.question: A KPI (key performance indicator) is BEST described as:
options: A measurable value that shows how effectively a project is achieving key objectives
A list of all project stakeholders
questions.explanation:
A measurable value that shows how effectively a project is achieving key objectives defines a KPI, used to track performance against targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
A list of all project stakeholders: a stakeholder list is a register, not a performance metric.
A type of risk response: a KPI measures performance, it is not a strategy for handling risk.
A contractual penalty clause: penalties appear in contracts and SLAs, but a KPI is a measurement indicator.

questions.question: A company sets an ambitious objective with three measurable key results to track progress toward it each quarter. This goal-setting framework is known as:
questions.explanation:
OKR (Objectives and Key Results) pairs an ambitious objective with measurable key results to track progress, typically quarterly.

Why the other options are wrong:
KPI: a KPI is a single performance indicator, not the objective-plus-key-results framework.
SLA: an SLA defines service commitments between provider and customer, not internal goal-setting.
RACI: RACI is a responsibility assignment matrix, unrelated to setting objectives and key results.

questions.question: During quality management, verification confirms the product was built correctly to specification, while validation confirms the right product was built to meet the customer's needs. A team runs the software against documented requirements to confirm each was implemented. This activity is:
questions.explanation:
Verification checks the product against documented requirements and specifications to confirm it was built correctly.

Why the other options are wrong:
Validation: validation confirms the product meets the customer's actual needs, which is broader than checking against documented specs.
A retrospective: a retrospective reviews process improvement, not whether requirements were implemented.
A procurement audit: a procurement audit reviews contracts and vendor processes, not product requirements.

questions.question: An independent team reviews a project's processes and deliverables to ensure compliance with standards and policies. This activity is BEST described as a:
questions.explanation:
A Quality audit is an independent, structured review verifying that project activities comply with organizational policies, processes, and standards.

Why the other options are wrong:
Retrospective: a retrospective is a team-led reflection on improvement, not an independent compliance review.
Sprint review: a sprint review demonstrates the increment to stakeholders, not a compliance audit.
Kickoff meeting: a kickoff launches the project and aligns the team, unrelated to auditing standards compliance.

questions.question: A vendor's SLA promises 99.9% uptime. Over a month the service was down long enough to fall to 99.5%. As PM, what is the BEST first action?
options: Ignore it since the service is mostly up
Document the SLA breach and invoke the agreed remedies or penalties
questions.explanation:
The PM should Document the SLA breach and invoke the agreed remedies or penalties, holding the vendor accountable per the contract terms.

Why the other options are wrong:
Cancel the entire project: canceling is a disproportionate reaction to a single SLA shortfall.
Ignore it since the service is mostly up: ignoring a documented breach forfeits contractual remedies and accountability.
Increase the project budget: raising the budget does not address the vendor's failure to meet the agreed service level.

questions.question: A project manager wants a metric that measures the customer's satisfaction with delivered value rather than internal output counts. Which is the BEST choice?
options: Total hours logged by the team
A KPI tied to customer satisfaction or value delivered
Number of lines of code written
questions.explanation:
A KPI tied to customer satisfaction or value delivered measures outcomes that matter to the customer, aligning with the goal of tracking value.

Why the other options are wrong:
Number of lines of code written: lines of code is an output count that does not reflect customer satisfaction or value.
Total hours logged by the team: hours logged measures effort, not the value or satisfaction the customer receives.
Count of meetings held: counting meetings is an activity metric with no link to delivered value.

questions.question: What does validation in verification and validation (V&V) primarily confirm?
options: That the right product was built to meet the customer's needs
That the team followed the schedule
That the budget was not exceeded
questions.explanation:
Validation confirms That the right product was built to meet the customer's needs, ensuring the deliverable provides the intended value.

Why the other options are wrong:
That the team followed the schedule: schedule adherence is a performance measure, not the purpose of validation.
That the budget was not exceeded: budget control is a cost concern, separate from validating the product fits needs.
That all meetings were attended: meeting attendance has nothing to do with confirming the product meets customer needs.

questions.question: A project team consistently meets its sprint goals but customer satisfaction surveys remain low. Which performance measurement insight BEST explains this gap?
options: The WBS has too many levels
Output metrics are being met but outcome/value metrics are not
The SLA penalties are too high
questions.explanation:
Output metrics are being met but outcome/value metrics are not explains the gap: the team produces deliverables yet fails to deliver the value customers actually want.

Why the other options are wrong:
The team has no velocity: meeting sprint goals shows the team does have velocity, so this is contradicted.
The SLA penalties are too high: SLA penalties relate to service contracts, not the output-versus-outcome gap in satisfaction.
The WBS has too many levels: WBS depth is a scope structuring detail unrelated to customer satisfaction outcomes.

questions.question: A project has 6 stakeholders who all communicate with each other. Using the formula n(n-1)/2, how many communication channels exist?
questions.explanation:
15 is correct because 6(6-1)/2 = 6 times 5 divided by 2 = 30 / 2 = 15 communication channels.

Why the other options are wrong:
12: 12 does not result from the n(n-1)/2 formula for 6 stakeholders.
30: 30 is the numerator 6 times 5 before dividing by 2.
6: 6 is simply the number of stakeholders, not the number of channels between them.

questions.question: An urgent issue requires immediate two-way discussion and quick resolution with a remote stakeholder. Which communication method is MOST appropriate?
options: A synchronous phone or video call
A note added to next month's newsletter
A formal written report mailed next week
A post on a public forum
questions.explanation:
A synchronous phone or video call enables immediate two-way discussion, ideal for urgent issues needing quick resolution.

Why the other options are wrong:
A formal written report mailed next week: a mailed report is far too slow for an urgent matter.
A note added to next month's newsletter: a monthly newsletter cannot resolve an issue requiring immediate attention.
A post on a public forum: a public forum is inappropriate for an urgent, direct stakeholder discussion.

questions.question: Sending a status report by email to many stakeholders without expecting an immediate response is an example of which communication method?
questions.explanation:
Push communication sends information to specific recipients, such as emailing a status report, without ensuring they read it immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
Interactive communication: interactive communication is real-time, multidirectional exchange like a meeting or call, not a one-way email.
Pull communication: pull communication lets recipients retrieve information at will, such as from a portal, rather than being sent to them.
Nonverbal communication: nonverbal communication refers to body language and tone, not the email distribution method.

questions.question: Posting project documents to a shared repository where stakeholders access them on their own initiative is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Pull communication places information in a shared location, such as a portal or repository, where recipients retrieve it at their own discretion.

Why the other options are wrong:
Push communication: push communication actively sends information to recipients rather than letting them retrieve it.
Interactive communication: interactive communication is real-time two-way exchange, not self-service access.
Escalation: escalation is raising an issue to higher authority, not a method of distributing documents.

questions.question: A stakeholder analysis shows one stakeholder has high power and high interest in the project. According to the power/interest grid, how should the PM engage this stakeholder?
options: Manage closely with active, frequent engagement
questions.explanation:
High-power, high-interest stakeholders should be Manage closely with active, frequent engagement because their influence and interest make them critical to success.

Why the other options are wrong:
Monitor with minimal effort: minimal monitoring applies to low-power, low-interest stakeholders, not this critical one.
Keep satisfied with periodic updates: keeping satisfied applies to high-power but low-interest stakeholders, not those with high interest.
Ignore until the project ends: ignoring a powerful, interested stakeholder risks serious resistance and project failure.

questions.question: Communicating differently with a technical engineering team versus an executive sponsor is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Adjusting message content, detail, and format for different audiences is Tailoring communication to the audience, a core communication best practice.

Why the other options are wrong:
Ignoring stakeholders: tailoring engages stakeholders appropriately, the opposite of ignoring them.
Avoiding documentation: adapting communication does not mean skipping documentation.
Reducing the schedule: communication tailoring has nothing to do with compressing the schedule.

questions.question: Which communication barrier is MOST likely when team members speak different native languages and work across cultures?
options: Misinterpretation due to language and cultural differences
questions.explanation:
Misinterpretation due to language and cultural differences is a common communication barrier on multicultural teams, requiring deliberate clarity.

Why the other options are wrong:
A blocked critical path: a blocked critical path is a schedule problem, not a communication barrier.
An over-allocated resource: over-allocation is a resource management issue, not a language barrier.
A missed milestone: a missed milestone is a schedule symptom, not a communication barrier itself.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a meeting agenda?
options: To outline the topics, objectives, and time allocation so the meeting stays focused
questions.explanation:
An agenda exists To outline the topics, objectives, and time allocation so the meeting stays focused and productive.

Why the other options are wrong:
To replace the project schedule: an agenda guides a single meeting, it does not replace the project schedule.
To document project risks: risks are tracked in the risk register, not a meeting agenda.
To assign the project budget: budgets are set during cost planning, not by a meeting agenda.

questions.question: Why should a project manager identify required attendees and their roles before scheduling a meeting?
options: To eliminate the need for minutes
To ensure the right decision-makers are present and the meeting is productive
questions.explanation:
Identifying attendees ensures To ensure the right decision-makers are present and the meeting is productive, so decisions can actually be made.

Why the other options are wrong:
To increase the meeting length: the goal is an efficient meeting, not a longer one.
To avoid creating an agenda: identifying attendees complements an agenda, it does not replace the need for one.
To eliminate the need for minutes: minutes are still needed to record outcomes regardless of who attends.

questions.question: Distributing the agenda to attendees before a meeting primarily helps to:
options: Let attendees prepare so the meeting is more efficient
questions.explanation:
Sending the agenda in advance helps Let attendees prepare so the meeting is more efficient, improving the quality of discussion.

Why the other options are wrong:
Make the meeting longer: preparation aims to shorten and focus the meeting, not lengthen it.
Replace the meeting minutes: an agenda guides the meeting beforehand, while minutes record it afterward; they are not interchangeable.
Avoid identifying decision-makers: distributing an agenda does not remove the need to identify the right attendees.

questions.question: In a RACI matrix, best practice is to have how many people accountable (A) for any single task?
questions.explanation:
Exactly one person should be accountable for each task so there is a single, clear point of ownership and decision authority.

Why the other options are wrong:
At least three: multiple accountable people blur ownership and cause confusion over who is answerable.
As many as possible: spreading accountability widely destroys the clarity RACI is meant to provide.
Zero: a task with no accountable person has no clear owner, risking it being neglected.

questions.question: A project manager identifies that the team lacks a needed skill. According to the resource life cycle, what is the appropriate phase to address this through training or hiring?
questions.explanation:
Acquire and develop resources is the phase where the PM brings on and trains team members, directly addressing a skill gap.

Why the other options are wrong:
Resource release: release occurs when resources are no longer needed, not when acquiring or developing skills.
Resource retirement: retirement removes a resource at end of use, the opposite of developing new skills.
Closing: closing finalizes the project, not the point to acquire or train resources.

questions.question: A critical resource is over-allocated, scheduled to work on two tasks at the same time. Which technique adjusts the schedule to resolve this resource conflict, even if it delays the finish?
questions.explanation:
Resource leveling adjusts the schedule to resolve over-allocation by ensuring resources are not double-booked, which can extend the finish date.

Why the other options are wrong:
Fast tracking: fast tracking overlaps activities to shorten the schedule but does not resolve resource over-allocation.
Crashing: crashing adds resources to shorten duration, not to fix a person being double-booked.
Scope creep: scope creep is uncontrolled scope growth, not a scheduling technique.

questions.question: At the end of a project, team members are reassigned to other work and equipment is returned. Which resource life cycle phase does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Release is the resource life cycle phase where team members and equipment are returned or reassigned once they are no longer needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
Acquire: acquire is when resources are first brought onto the project, the opposite of releasing them.
Develop: develop builds team skills and cohesion during the project, not the end-of-use return.
Plan: plan determines what resources will be needed, before they are ever acquired or released.

questions.question: A project manager wants to build team cohesion and improve individual competencies during execution. Per the resource life cycle, this corresponds to which activity?
questions.explanation:
Developing the team focuses on improving competencies, interaction, and cohesion so the team performs better during execution.

Why the other options are wrong:
Releasing resources: releasing returns resources at the end and does not build skills or cohesion.
Procuring vendors: procuring vendors is a purchasing activity, not internal team development.
Closing the project: closing finalizes the project rather than developing the team mid-execution.

questions.question: A buyer wants vendors to propose a complete solution, including their approach, qualifications, and pricing for a complex need. Which document should be issued?
questions.explanation:
An RFP (Request for Proposal) asks vendors to propose a full solution including approach, qualifications, and pricing for a complex requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
RFQ: an RFQ only requests pricing for a well-defined item, not a full proposed solution.
RFI: an RFI collects preliminary information, not detailed competitive proposals.
Purchase order: a purchase order is a buying instrument issued after selection, not a solicitation for proposals.

questions.question: A project's scope is uncertain and likely to evolve, and the buyer needs flexibility to pay for actual labor hours and materials as work proceeds. Which contract type is MOST suitable?
questions.explanation:
A Time and materials contract pays for actual labor hours and materials, giving flexibility when scope is uncertain and may evolve.

Why the other options are wrong:
Firm-fixed-price: a firm-fixed-price contract requires well-defined scope and would be risky when requirements are still evolving.
Lump-sum: a lump-sum (fixed-price) arrangement locks one total price and lacks the flexibility uncertain scope demands.
Fixed-price-incentive-fee: this fixed-price variant still presumes a defined scope, unsuitable for evolving requirements.

questions.question: In a cost-reimbursable contract, the seller is paid for legitimate actual costs plus an additional fee. Which party bears the GREATER cost risk in this arrangement?
questions.explanation:
In a cost-reimbursable contract, The buyer bears greater cost risk because they reimburse the seller's actual costs, which can exceed initial estimates.

Why the other options are wrong:
The seller: the seller's costs are reimbursed, so the seller carries less risk than in a fixed-price arrangement.
Neither party bears risk: every contract allocates cost risk; here it falls mainly on the buyer.
The change control board: the CCB governs changes and is not a contractual party bearing cost risk.

questions.question: A finance team evaluates a project by discounting all future cash inflows and outflows back to today's value and summing them. Which financial metric are they calculating?
questions.explanation:
Net present value (NPV) discounts all future cash flows to present value and sums them, with a positive result indicating value creation.

Why the other options are wrong:
Payback period: payback measures how long until the investment is recovered, not the discounted sum of cash flows.
Return on investment (ROI): ROI is a simple ratio of gain to cost and does not discount cash flows over time.
Internal rate of return (IRR): IRR finds the discount rate that makes NPV zero, not the discounted total itself.

questions.question: Two competing projects are compared. Management selects the one with the higher discount rate at which net present value equals zero. Which metric drove this decision?
questions.explanation:
Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero, and a higher IRR signals a more attractive investment.

Why the other options are wrong:
Net present value: NPV is a dollar amount at a chosen discount rate, not the rate that zeroes out NPV.
Payback period: payback measures recovery time and ignores the discount rate entirely.
Return on investment: ROI is a percentage gain on cost and does not identify the break-even discount rate.

questions.question: A project requires a $60,000 investment and is forecast to generate $20,000 in net cash inflow each year. Using the simple payback method, when is the investment recovered?
questions.explanation:
In 3 years is correct because $60,000 divided by $20,000 per year equals a three-year payback period.

Why the other options are wrong:
In 2 years: two years recovers only $40,000, leaving $20,000 unrecovered.
In 4 years: four years would recover $80,000, overshooting the $60,000 investment by a year.
In 6 years: six years assumes roughly $10,000 annual inflow, which contradicts the stated $20,000.

questions.question: During the concept phase, the project manager discovers an existing master service agreement with a supplier that already covers the goods the new project needs. How should this preexisting contract influence the discovery work?
options: It must be ignored because each project requires a brand-new contract
It can be leveraged to reduce procurement time and cost for the new project
It automatically cancels the need for a business case
It forces the project to use a different supplier
questions.explanation:
It can be leveraged to reduce procurement time and cost for the new project because an existing master service agreement already establishes terms the project can reuse.

Why the other options are wrong:
It must be ignored because each project requires a brand-new contract: reusing valid existing contracts is a recognized way to save time, so ignoring it is wasteful.
It automatically cancels the need for a business case: the business case justifies the project regardless of which contracts exist.
It forces the project to use a different supplier: an existing agreement enables, rather than prohibits, using that same supplier.

questions.question: Before a project is formally approved, who is typically responsible for developing and presenting the business case to leadership?
questions.explanation:
The project sponsor or initiator develops and presents the business case to leadership to secure approval and funding.

Why the other options are wrong:
The end users: end users provide requirements but do not own the business case justification to leadership.
The procurement clerk: procurement handles purchasing tasks and does not champion the project's justification.
The closing committee: closure activities occur at the end of a project, not during concept justification.

questions.question: A discovery analysis concludes that a project's net present value is negative even though its payback period seems short. What does the negative NPV indicate?
options: The payback period calculation is invalid
The project creates value over time
The project's discounted cash flows do not exceed the investment
The internal rate of return must be very high
questions.explanation:
The project's discounted cash flows do not exceed the investment is what a negative NPV signals, meaning the project destroys value at the chosen discount rate.

Why the other options are wrong:
The project creates value over time: value creation is shown by a positive NPV, not a negative one.
The payback period calculation is invalid: payback and NPV are independent measures, so a short payback does not make NPV invalid.
The internal rate of return must be very high: a negative NPV at the chosen rate implies the IRR is below that rate, not high.

questions.question: A sponsor wants the discovery documentation to capture the high-level reason the project exists, its expected benefits, and the consequences of not doing it. Which section of the business case addresses the consequences of inaction?
questions.explanation:
Alternatives and 'do nothing' option is the business case section that evaluates other approaches, including the consequences of taking no action.

Why the other options are wrong:
Cost-benefit analysis: the cost-benefit analysis quantifies value but does not specifically describe the impact of doing nothing.
Detailed WBS: a WBS is a planning artifact for approved work, not part of justifying the concept.
Closeout report: a closeout report summarizes results at project end, unrelated to discovery alternatives.

questions.question: Two projects each cost $100,000. Project A returns $130,000 in undiscounted benefits; Project B returns $125,000 but recovers its cost in half the time. If the organization values rapid cash recovery above all, which metric most supports choosing Project B?
questions.explanation:
Shorter payback period directly favors Project B because the organization prioritizes recovering its investment quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
Higher ROI: Project A has the higher ROI with greater total benefit, so ROI would favor A, not B.
Larger NPV: a larger NPV again tends to favor the higher-benefit Project A, not the faster-recovering B.
Lower IRR: a lower IRR is undesirable and would never be the basis for selecting a project.

questions.question: In the concept phase, a project manager evaluates whether the organization has the technical skills, funding, and time to deliver a proposed solution. This evaluation is BEST described as a:
questions.explanation:
Feasibility analysis assesses whether the organization has the skills, funding, and time to deliver the proposed solution before committing.

Why the other options are wrong:
Lessons learned review: lessons learned are gathered at closure to improve future projects, not to assess feasibility up front.
Sign-off: sign-off is formal acceptance of deliverables, which occurs much later than concept feasibility.
Phase gate closure: a phase gate evaluates readiness to advance between phases, not the initial feasibility of the concept.

questions.question: During discovery, leadership asks the project manager to compare three vendor solutions on cost, capability, and risk before any project is chartered. This comparison most directly supports which outcome?
options: Selecting the best alternative for the business case
questions.explanation:
Selecting the best alternative for the business case is the purpose of comparing vendor solutions on cost, capability, and risk during discovery.

Why the other options are wrong:
Closing existing contracts: closing contracts is a closing-phase procurement task, not a discovery comparison.
Releasing project resources: releasing resources happens at closure after work is complete.
Reconciling the final budget: budget reconciliation is a closeout activity, not part of selecting a concept.

questions.question: A project's business case shows a positive NPV, an IRR above the company's required rate, and a payback within the policy limit, yet the steering committee rejects it. Which factor BEST explains a justified rejection despite favorable financials?
options: ROI is always more important than NPV
The project does not align with strategic objectives or has unacceptable non-financial risk
Payback period must always be under one year
questions.explanation:
The project does not align with strategic objectives or has unacceptable non-financial risk can justify rejecting a financially sound project, since selection considers strategy and risk, not numbers alone.

Why the other options are wrong:
The financial metrics were miscalculated: the scenario states the metrics are favorable, so assuming miscalculation contradicts the facts given.
ROI is always more important than NPV: no single metric automatically dominates; selection weighs many factors.
Payback period must always be under one year: there is no universal one-year payback rule, and the case already met policy limits.

questions.question: A discovery team documents the expected tangible benefit of reducing manual processing labor by $30,000 annually. This figure is BEST categorized in the business case as a:
questions.explanation:
Quantifiable benefit describes a measurable monetary gain such as $30,000 in annual labor savings.

Why the other options are wrong:
Intangible benefit: intangible benefits like improved morale cannot be expressed as a precise dollar figure.
Sunk cost: a sunk cost is money already spent and unrecoverable, not a future benefit.
Contingency reserve: a contingency reserve is budget set aside for known risks, not a benefit projection.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an intangible benefit that might appear in a business case?
options: Improved customer satisfaction and brand reputation
questions.explanation:
Improved customer satisfaction and brand reputation is an intangible benefit because it provides value that is real but hard to quantify in dollars.

Why the other options are wrong:
A $25,000 reduction in licensing fees: this is a precise monetary saving, making it a tangible benefit.
A 15% decrease in hardware costs: a measurable percentage cost reduction is tangible, not intangible.
$10,000 saved in overtime pay: a specific dollar saving is a quantifiable, tangible benefit.

questions.question: A sponsor states that the project must be completed before a new regulation takes effect or the company faces fines. In the business case, this regulatory deadline is BEST captured as a:
questions.explanation:
Business driver or justification captures the regulatory deadline because it is the underlying reason compelling the project to proceed.

Why the other options are wrong:
Work package: a work package is a unit of work in the WBS during planning, not a concept-phase driver.
Quality metric: a quality metric measures deliverable conformance, not the reason for doing the project.
Resource calendar: a resource calendar shows availability of resources, unrelated to justifying the project.

questions.question: During discovery, a project manager learns that a preexisting contract with a vendor will expire in three months, before the project would need that vendor. What is the MOST appropriate action to reflect this in the concept analysis?
options: Flag the contract's expiration as a procurement risk and consider renewal or alternatives
Assume the contract will renew automatically and ignore it
Sign the project sponsor's name to extend it
questions.explanation:
Flag the contract's expiration as a procurement risk and consider renewal or alternatives is correct because an expiring contract that the project will rely on is a real risk needing proactive planning.

Why the other options are wrong:
Assume the contract will renew automatically and ignore it: assuming renewal without verification leaves the project exposed if it lapses.
Cancel the project immediately: an expiring contract is a manageable risk, not grounds to abandon a justified project.
Sign the project sponsor's name to extend it: signing on someone's behalf without authority is unethical and improper.

questions.question: During initiation, the project manager creates a high-level description of what the project will and will not include before detailed planning begins. This is known as the:
questions.explanation:
Preliminary scope statement is the high-level initiation description of what the project will and will not include before detailed planning.

Why the other options are wrong:
Detailed WBS: a WBS is produced during planning and decomposes work far beyond a preliminary high-level scope.
Quality assurance plan: the QA plan defines quality processes during planning, not the early scope boundaries.
Budget baseline: the budget baseline is an approved cost plan set during planning, not an initiation scope description.

questions.question: During initiation, the project manager analyzes each stakeholder's level of interest, influence, and attitude toward the project. The PRIMARY purpose of this assessment is to:
options: Determine how to engage and communicate with each stakeholder
questions.explanation:
Determine how to engage and communicate with each stakeholder is the purpose of assessing stakeholder interest, influence, and attitude.

Why the other options are wrong:
Calculate the project budget: budgeting is a cost-planning task, not a stakeholder engagement analysis.
Define the test plan: test planning is a quality execution activity, not stakeholder assessment.
Close out the contracts: contract closure is a closing-phase procurement task, unrelated to stakeholder analysis.

questions.question: A project manager wants to classify stakeholders so that high-influence, high-interest parties receive the most attention. Which technique supports this prioritization?
questions.explanation:
Power/interest grid classifies stakeholders by their power and interest so the most influential and interested receive the greatest engagement.

Why the other options are wrong:
Critical path method: the critical path method analyzes schedule duration, not stakeholder prioritization.
Earned value analysis: earned value measures cost and schedule performance, not stakeholder importance.
Pareto chart: a Pareto chart ranks causes of problems by frequency, not stakeholders by influence.

questions.question: During initiation a key stakeholder is identified as high influence but currently opposed to the project. According to good stakeholder management, what is the MOST appropriate initial response?
options: Engage them early to understand and address their concerns
Escalate immediately to terminate their involvement
questions.explanation:
Engage them early to understand and address their concerns is best because a high-influence opponent can derail the project unless their concerns are addressed proactively.

Why the other options are wrong:
Exclude them from all communications: excluding a powerful stakeholder increases the risk they will undermine the project.
Escalate immediately to terminate their involvement: terminating involvement is rarely possible or wise for a high-influence party and skips dialogue.
Ignore their opposition until execution: ignoring opposition lets concerns fester and surface at a costlier time.

questions.question: Who should typically attend a project kickoff meeting?
options: Key stakeholders, team members, and the sponsor
questions.explanation:
Key stakeholders, team members, and the sponsor should attend the kickoff to align everyone on objectives and roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
Only the project manager: a kickoff is about aligning many parties, so the PM alone defeats its purpose.
Only external auditors: auditors are not the audience for an alignment kickoff.
Only the closing committee: a closing committee operates at project end, not at kickoff.

questions.question: During initiation, the project manager documents that certain assumptions, such as the availability of a specialized contractor, underpin the preliminary scope. Where are such assumptions and constraints BEST recorded?
options: In the project charter and assumption log
questions.explanation:
In the project charter and assumption log is where initiation-phase assumptions and constraints are documented so they can be tracked.

Why the other options are wrong:
In the final closeout report: the closeout report is produced at the end, not where initial assumptions belong.
In the vendor invoice: a vendor invoice is a billing document, not a place to record project assumptions.
In the lessons learned archive: lessons learned capture retrospective insights, not current initiation assumptions.

questions.question: A project manager realizes that the access requirements identified during initiation were never provisioned, and the team cannot start work on day one. What does this MOST clearly reflect a failure to do during initiation?
options: Translate identified access requirements into actual provisioning before execution
questions.explanation:
Translate identified access requirements into actual provisioning before execution was the missed step, since identifying access is only useful if it is acted upon before work begins.

Why the other options are wrong:
Calculate earned value: earned value is an execution performance measure unrelated to provisioning access.
Conduct lessons learned: lessons learned occur at closure and would not have provisioned access on day one.
Reconcile the budget: budget reconciliation is a closing task, not the cause of unprovisioned access.

questions.question: A project manager wants stakeholders to know early how decisions will be escalated and who has final authority. Capturing the decision-making hierarchy during initiation primarily helps with:
questions.explanation:
Governance and clear escalation paths is the benefit of documenting the decision-making hierarchy early in the project.

Why the other options are wrong:
Calculating the schedule variance: schedule variance is an earned value metric, not a governance structure.
Archiving closed records: archiving is a closing activity unrelated to escalation paths.
Releasing the project team: releasing the team happens at closure, not during governance setup.

questions.question: A reserve controlled by senior management for unforeseen work that is outside the project's cost baseline is known as the:
questions.explanation:
Management reserve is held by senior management for unforeseen 'unknown unknown' work and sits outside the cost baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
Contingency reserve: contingency reserve covers identified risks and is included within the cost baseline.
Quality budget: a quality budget funds quality activities, not unforeseen scope.
Communication budget: a communication budget funds reporting and information flow, not unforeseen work.

questions.question: During planning, the project manager catalogs all the people, equipment, and materials available for assignment to the project. This catalog is the:
questions.explanation:
Resource pool is the catalog of people, equipment, and materials available for assignment to the project.

Why the other options are wrong:
Cost baseline: the cost baseline is the approved time-phased budget, not a list of available resources.
Quality plan: the quality plan defines quality standards and processes, not resource availability.
Phase gate: a phase gate is a checkpoint between phases, unrelated to cataloging resources.

questions.question: During planning, the project manager conducts an initial risk assessment. What is the PRIMARY output of this activity?
options: A risk register of identified risks with analysis and responses
questions.explanation:
A risk register of identified risks with analysis and responses is the primary output of an initial risk assessment.

Why the other options are wrong:
A signed acceptance form: acceptance forms are produced when deliverables are validated, not during risk assessment.
An archived closeout report: a closeout report is a closing artifact, not a risk planning output.
A vendor invoice: a vendor invoice is a billing document unrelated to risk planning.

questions.question: A project manager combines the scope, schedule, cost, quality, communication, risk, and procurement subsidiary plans into one comprehensive document that guides execution. This overarching document is the:
questions.explanation:
Project management plan integrates all subsidiary plans into one comprehensive document that guides execution and control.

Why the other options are wrong:
Business case: the business case justifies the project in discovery and is not the integrated execution plan.
Status dashboard: a status dashboard reports progress, not the integrated plan itself.
Lessons learned register: the lessons learned register captures retrospective insights, not the planning blueprint.

questions.question: When building the budget, a project manager aggregates the estimated costs of each work package and adds contingency reserves. The result, once approved, becomes the:
questions.explanation:
Cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget formed by aggregating work package estimates plus contingency reserves.

Why the other options are wrong:
Communication plan: the communication plan governs information flow, not the approved budget.
Resource pool: a resource pool lists available resources, not the aggregated cost figure.
Phase gate: a phase gate is a checkpoint between phases, unrelated to the budget baseline.

questions.question: A project manager must define units of work small enough to be reliably estimated yet large enough to manage efficiently. Decomposing the WBS too far would MOST likely cause:
options: A higher internal rate of return
Excessive overhead in tracking and managing tiny components
questions.explanation:
Excessive overhead in tracking and managing tiny components results from decomposing the WBS too far, which wastes effort on micromanagement.

Why the other options are wrong:
A larger contingency reserve: reserve size is driven by risk, not by how finely the WBS is decomposed.
A higher internal rate of return: IRR is a financial metric unaffected by WBS granularity.
Loss of the project charter: the charter is unaffected by how the WBS is decomposed.

questions.question: A project manager has the scope statement and WBS but no time-phased view of when costs will be incurred across the project. Which planning output BEST provides this view?
questions.explanation:
The time-phased cost baseline (S-curve) shows planned spending over time, providing the view of when costs will be incurred.

Why the other options are wrong:
The stakeholder register: the stakeholder register lists parties, not the spending profile over time.
The kickoff agenda: a kickoff agenda organizes a meeting and shows no cost timeline.
The lessons learned report: lessons learned are retrospective and do not project future spending.

questions.question: A project has an earned value (EV) of $75,000 and an actual cost (AC) of $100,000. What is the cost performance index (CPI), and how should it be interpreted?
options: CPI = 25,000, the project is over budget
CPI = 0.75, the project is spending more than it earns
CPI = 1.0, the project is exactly on budget
CPI = 1.33, the project is under budget
questions.explanation:
CPI = 0.75, the project is spending more than it earns because CPI equals EV divided by AC ($75,000 / $100,000), and a value below 1.0 indicates cost overrun.

Why the other options are wrong:
CPI = 1.33, the project is under budget: 1.33 would result from dividing AC by EV, which inverts the formula.
CPI = 1.0, the project is exactly on budget: a CPI of 1.0 requires EV to equal AC, which it does not here.
CPI = 25,000, the project is over budget: 25,000 is the cost variance amount, not the index ratio.

questions.question: A project has an earned value (EV) of $120,000 and a planned value (PV) of $100,000. What is the schedule performance index (SPI), and what does it indicate?
options: SPI = 1.2, the project is ahead of schedule
SPI = 20,000, the project is on schedule
SPI = 1.0, the project is over budget
SPI = 0.83, the project is behind schedule
questions.explanation:
SPI = 1.2, the project is ahead of schedule because SPI equals EV divided by PV ($120,000 / $100,000), and a value above 1.0 means work is ahead of plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
SPI = 0.83, the project is behind schedule: 0.83 results from dividing PV by EV, inverting the formula.
SPI = 20,000, the project is on schedule: 20,000 is the schedule variance amount, not the index.
SPI = 1.0, the project is over budget: SPI of 1.0 would require EV to equal PV, and SPI concerns schedule, not budget.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $200,000 and a current cost performance index (CPI) of 0.80. Assuming performance continues at this rate, what is the estimate at completion (EAC) using EAC = BAC / CPI?
questions.explanation:
$250,000 is correct because EAC equals BAC divided by CPI, or $200,000 / 0.80, which forecasts a higher final cost due to poor performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
$160,000: this multiplies BAC by 0.80 instead of dividing, wrongly forecasting a cost reduction.
$200,000: $200,000 is the original BAC and ignores the unfavorable CPI of 0.80.
$240,000: $240,000 does not result from BAC divided by 0.80 and has no formula basis.

questions.question: During execution, a project manager mediates between two team members whose disagreement over technical approach is delaying work. Resolving this disagreement is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Conflict management is the practice of resolving disagreements among team members to keep work progressing.

Why the other options are wrong:
Earned value analysis: earned value analysis measures cost and schedule performance, not interpersonal disputes.
Budget reconciliation: budget reconciliation is a closing financial task, unrelated to mediating conflict.
Scope decomposition: scope decomposition is a planning activity to build the WBS, not conflict resolution.

questions.question: During execution, a project manager regularly distributes status reports comparing actual progress to the baseline. This activity is BEST categorized as:
questions.explanation:
Tracking and reporting covers monitoring actual progress against the baseline and communicating it through status reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
Closing contracts: closing contracts is a closing-phase procurement task, not progress reporting.
Releasing resources: releasing resources occurs at closure, not during ongoing reporting.
Defining scope: defining scope is a planning activity, not execution tracking.

questions.question: A project shows CPI = 1.10 and SPI = 0.85. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The project is under budget and ahead of schedule
The project is over budget and behind schedule
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule
The project is under budget but behind schedule
questions.explanation:
The project is under budget but behind schedule is correct because a CPI above 1.0 means cost efficiency is favorable while an SPI below 1.0 means work is behind plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule: this reverses both indices; CPI above 1.0 is under budget and SPI below 1.0 is behind schedule.
The project is over budget and behind schedule: CPI above 1.0 indicates under budget, not over.
The project is under budget and ahead of schedule: SPI of 0.85 is below 1.0, so the project is behind, not ahead.

questions.question: Which earned value term represents the budgeted cost of the work actually completed at a point in time?
questions.explanation:
Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of the work actually completed at a given point in time.

Why the other options are wrong:
Planned value (PV): PV is the budgeted cost of work scheduled to be done, not work actually completed.
Actual cost (AC): AC is the real money spent on completed work, not its budgeted value.
Budget at completion (BAC): BAC is the total approved budget for the entire project, not the value of work done so far.

questions.question: A project's earned value (EV) is $50,000, planned value (PV) is $60,000, and actual cost (AC) is $55,000. Which statement is correct?
options: The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The project is on schedule and on budget
The project is both behind schedule (SV negative) and over budget (CV negative)
The project is behind schedule but under budget
questions.explanation:
The project is both behind schedule (SV negative) and over budget (CV negative) because SV = EV - PV = -$10,000 and CV = EV - AC = -$5,000, both negative.

Why the other options are wrong:
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget: both variances are negative, so it is neither ahead nor under.
The project is on schedule and on budget: on schedule and on budget would require both variances to be zero, which they are not.
The project is behind schedule but under budget: CV is negative ($50,000 - $55,000), so the project is over budget, not under.

questions.question: During execution, the project manager updates the timeline after a critical task finishes two days late, recalculating downstream task dates. This activity is BEST described as:
options: Updating the schedule to reflect actual progress
questions.explanation:
Updating the schedule to reflect actual progress is the activity of recalculating downstream dates after a task slips during execution.

Why the other options are wrong:
Reconciling the final budget: budget reconciliation is a closing activity, not schedule updating.
Validating deliverables: validating deliverables is acceptance at closing, not adjusting the timeline.
Closing the contract: closing a contract is a procurement closure task, unrelated to schedule recalculation.

questions.question: A project manager has CPI = 0.90 and wants to forecast the remaining cost to finish, assuming current efficiency continues. Which earned value figure should the project manager calculate?
questions.explanation:
Estimate to complete (ETC) forecasts the cost of the remaining work, which is exactly what the project manager wants to know.

Why the other options are wrong:
Planned value (PV): PV is the budgeted cost of scheduled work, not a forecast of remaining cost.
Schedule variance (SV): SV measures schedule performance, not the cost remaining to finish.
Budget at completion (BAC): BAC is the original total budget, not a forecast adjusted for current efficiency.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a project closure meeting?
options: To formally confirm completion and review project results with stakeholders
questions.explanation:
To formally confirm completion and review project results with stakeholders is the purpose of a closure meeting.

Why the other options are wrong:
To authorize the project: authorization occurs in initiation via the charter, not at closure.
To create the detailed WBS: the WBS is built in planning, not during the closure meeting.
To assess vendor prequalification: vendor prequalification is a discovery or procurement activity, not closure.

questions.question: At closing, the project manager stores all final project documents in a central, retrievable repository for future reference and audits. This activity is called:
questions.explanation:
Archiving stores final project documents in a central, retrievable repository for future reference and audits.

Why the other options are wrong:
Crashing: crashing is a schedule-compression technique, not document storage.
Fast tracking: fast tracking overlaps activities to shorten the schedule, unrelated to archiving.
Decomposing: decomposing breaks scope into smaller parts during planning, not storing records.

questions.question: A project manager has reconciled the budget, released the team, archived records, and held the closure meeting, but the closeout report has not been distributed to stakeholders. Why is distributing it still important?
options: It formally communicates final results and confirms closure to all stakeholders
It reopens the project for additional work
It is unnecessary once the team is released
It replaces the lessons learned register
questions.explanation:
It formally communicates final results and confirms closure to all stakeholders is why distributing the closeout report matters, ensuring everyone is informed the project is complete.

Why the other options are wrong:
It is unnecessary once the team is released: releasing the team does not inform stakeholders of final results.
It reopens the project for additional work: a closeout report concludes the project rather than reopening it.
It replaces the lessons learned register: the closeout report and lessons learned register serve different purposes and do not replace each other.

questions.question: During closing, the project manager verifies that the deliverables transitioned successfully to the operations team per the transition plan. This confirms:
options: The handover to ongoing support is complete
questions.explanation:
The handover to ongoing support is complete is what verifying the transition against the transition plan confirms at closing.

Why the other options are wrong:
The project budget was approved: budget approval is a planning and initiation matter, not transition verification.
The stakeholders were identified: stakeholder identification is an initiation activity, not a closing handover confirmation.
The WBS was decomposed correctly: WBS decomposition is a planning concern, unrelated to operations handover.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly reflects typical closing-phase activities for a completed project?
options: Release resources, perform feasibility analysis, sign the charter, then archive records
Archive records, validate deliverables, conduct kickoff, then release resources
Validate deliverables and obtain sign-off, close contracts, remove access and release resources, then archive records and capture lessons learned
Capture lessons learned, write the business case, validate deliverables, then close contracts
